subject: religious-studies

moments.title: Copernicus posthumous publication
moments.body: May 1543: 'De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium' published as Copernicus lies on his deathbed. The Sun, not the Earth, is the centre. The book includes a preface (by Andreas Osiander, without Copernicus's authority) presenting heliocentrism as a calculational hypothesis rather than physical truth.
moments.takeaway: The Copernican model was initially treated as a mathematical convenience by the church. Real trouble came when Galileo argued it was physically true.

moments.title: Sidereus Nuncius
moments.body: March 1610: Galileo publishes 'The Starry Messenger' describing telescope observations — mountains on the Moon, moons of Jupiter, phases of Venus. The phases of Venus are decisive evidence against the Ptolemaic model.
moments.takeaway: Galileo's observational evidence put the church in a position where the choice between Aristotelian-Ptolemaic and Copernican was scientific, not philosophical.

moments.title: Galileo's trial
moments.body: 22 June 1633: Galileo is condemned by the Inquisition for his 'Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems' (1632). He recants. House arrest until death (1642). The legend 'And yet it moves' (Eppur si muove) is later apocryphal.
moments.takeaway: Pope John Paul II in 1992 acknowledged that the church had erred in its treatment of Galileo. The reconciliation was 359 years coming.

now.title: Science and religion
now.body: The Galileo affair is the canonical case of religion-science conflict. Other examples (Darwin and creationism, contemporary debates over evolution in US schools, Vatican Observatory) extend or complicate it. The 'warfare' thesis (White, Draper, late 19th c.) has been substantially complicated by recent historians (Numbers, Brooke).
now.open_questions: Are religion and science fundamentally conflict-prone or compatible? Most contemporary historians (John Hedley Brooke 'Science and Religion', 1991) argue the relationship has been complex — sometimes conflict, often cooperation, mostly independence.

reflection: The Galileo case is more nuanced than popular narratives suggest. The church wasn't anti-science — it sponsored astronomy and natural philosophy — but it did claim authority over biblical interpretation and applied it to physical questions where it had no expertise. The lesson — that institutions overstep their competence — recurs.
